question: When a parameterized fixed-point algorithm is nonsmooth, do the derivatives propagated through its iterates converge to a meaningful derivative of the fixed-point map, at what rate, and which contraction and regularity assumptions make forward and reverse automatic differentiation valid?

key_findings.claim: The paper's central contribution is an infinite nonsmooth chain rule: under a uniformly contractive conservative Jacobian, set-valued piggyback derivatives approach a compact fixed attractor that is itself a conservative Jacobian of the solution map.
key_findings.evidence: For x_{k+1}=F(x_k,theta), every x-block A in the chosen conservative Jacobian J_F is assumed to have operator norm at most rho<1. The induced affine set map X -> {AX+B} is then contractive in Hausdorff distance and has a unique compact fixed set. Theorem 2 identifies the fixed set of J_F at the primal fixed point as a conservative Jacobian of theta -> xbar(theta), while Corollary 1 proves that the one-sided gap from the propagated derivative set J_{x_k} to this attractor tends to zero.

key_findings.claim: For almost every parameter, ordinary forward- and reverse-mode derivatives converge to the classical derivative of the fixed-point map, but this is an almost-everywhere asymptotic statement rather than a guarantee at a chosen kink or finite unrolling depth.
key_findings.evidence: Path-differentiable maps have singleton conservative Jacobians equal to their classical Jacobians almost everywhere. Taking the countable intersection of the full-measure differentiability sets for every iterate and the limit yields Corollary 2. Proposition 1 then translates Jacobian convergence into convergence of JVPs and, if the terminal cotangent converges, VJPs. At exceptional parameters, the paper guarantees only boundedness and that accumulation points lie in the set-valued attractor; it does not force a particular AD branch or a unique limit.

key_findings.claim: The convergence theorem is substantially narrower than convergence of the primal solver alone: it requires a selected conservative Jacobian whose entire x-block packet is contractive in operator norm.
key_findings.evidence: Assumption 1 is stronger than F_theta merely being contractive or an iteration merely converging. Every matrix A available in J_F(x,theta) must share a uniform rho<1 globally, with a local asymptotic relaxation only near the fixed point. The final conference version also explicitly assumes a conservative Jacobian for the initialization; the pinned arXiv v1 source uses J_{x_0} in PB and Algorithm 1 but omits that clause from Assumption 1. Noncontractive averaged maps, changing active-set derivatives, inertial state maps, and parameters at which AD chooses unstable generalized derivatives are not covered.

key_findings.claim: Nonsmooth piggyback differentiation can encode more limiting derivatives than pointwise implicit differentiation because repeated AD steps may combine different matrices from a generalized Jacobian packet.
key_findings.evidence: The implicit set {(I-A)^{-1}B} uses one coupled pair [A,B] at a time, whereas the affine fixed attractor is closed under repeated cross-compositions. Appendix C constructs a two-dimensional diagonal packet for which the implicit curve is strictly contained in the piggyback fixed set: applying one A to the fixed vector generated by another A produces (5/3,3/2), which no single lambda realizes in the implicit curve. Thus the piggyback limit remains conservative but need not equal the usual nonsmooth implicit formula at exceptional points.

key_findings.claim: For semialgebraic Lipschitz-gradient selections, the paper strengthens convergence to a linear rate through a local one-sided Lipschitz property of the selected conservative Jacobian.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3 shows that near x0, active selection indices at x are also active at x0, giving gap(J_F^s(x),J_F^s(x0)) <= L||x-x0||. Combining the primal rho^k contraction with the vanishing-perturbation set recursion yields Corollary 3's C(sqrt(rho)+epsilon)^k bound. The estimate is existential and local: C depends on theta and epsilon, no uniform finite-depth calibration is supplied, and the proof relies on a particular selection-based conservative Jacobian rather than every possible generalized derivative oracle.

key_findings.claim: The heavy-ball construction validly demonstrates that a linearly convergent nonsmooth primal iteration can have an unstable derivative product, although its appendix contains a false statement about the parameterized iterates.
key_findings.evidence: For the piecewise quadratic with curvatures 1 and 1/4 and beta=3/4, the two admissible state Jacobians have a four-step product with eigenvalue -9/8, so alternating branch implementations at theta=0 yield geometrically growing propagated derivatives while the primal trajectory remains at its optimum. Direct multiplication reproduces the printed eigenvalues -9/8 and -9/32. However, page 27 says x_k(theta)=y_k(theta)=theta for every theta and k from initialization x0=y0=theta even though the objective is independent of theta; already at theta=1 the first update is zero and the fourth is -9/8, not theta. The counterexample needs only the theta=0 trajectory, so this sentence is false but not fatal to the local derivative pathology.

key_findings.claim: The proximal-splitting applications illustrate the intended scope, but the Douglas-Rachford and ADMM appendix formulas are not reliable as printed.
key_findings.evidence: The forward-backward contraction argument is standard under strong convexity. In the Douglas-Rachford proof, page 24 says I+alpha A has eigenvalues below 1, though they exceed 1; Equations 24-25 subtract an identity matrix from the parameter blocks of reflected proximal Jacobians even when those blocks are p-by-m; and the displayed x-block E omits the one-half identity contribution required by one-half(I+R_f R_g). The ADMM derivation on page 25 then prints a dual g without the conjugate or transpose, writes phi(x) in a minimization over u, leaves an unrelated v in that objective, and omits the square on the second quadratic penalty. The standard cited Douglas-Rachford contraction and ADMM equivalence can repair the high-level application, but the displayed derivative construction is internally inconsistent.

key_findings.claim: The trend-filtering example is mislabeled in the pinned source and does not satisfy the stated strong-convexity argument under the symbols as written.
key_findings.evidence: The ADMM discussion requires phi to be strongly convex with Lipschitz gradient and A injective. Page 9 instead assigns psi(u)=lambda||u||_1 and calls it strongly convex, which is false, while assigning the squared data-fit to phi(v) and A=-I to u, swapping the function and variable roles from Equation 12. The final NeurIPS paper removes the false parenthetical but retains the swapped symbols. Renaming phi(u)=||u-theta||^2 with A=-I and psi(v)=lambda||v||_1 with B=D restores the intended standard splitting.

key_findings.claim: The official notebook does not faithfully reproduce the stated Ridge experiment and is order-dependent because it reuses a stale Lasso step-size variable.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines Ridge with theta||x||_2 squared. The notebook's ridge_xp instead computes max(0,1-lambda*mu/||x||)x, which is the proximal map of lambda||x||_2, not of the squared norm; the latter would be x/(1+2 lambda mu). Moreover the Ridge cell changes n,p and generates a new X but never recomputes Xnorm, so alpha=1.9/Xnorm uses the last Lasso replicate's 50-by-500 design. The stored notebook executed in that order and contains all six figure outputs without errors, but rerunning the Ridge section independently raises an undefined-name error and rerunning it after a different preceding cell changes the step size.

key_findings.claim: Several proof-level slips should be corrected before formal reuse, even though the underlying affine-contraction theorem has a short standard repair.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1's appendix restricts the hyperspace to a compact C containing the observed orbit but does not establish that the affine set map sends every nonempty closed subset of C back into C, which is needed for the stated Banach-Picard application; applying the standard completeness theorem directly to nonempty compact subsets of Euclidean space repairs this. Proposition 7 then writes X1=bar-J(X0) although the recursion gives J0(X0); only the inclusion in J_epsilon(X0) is needed. Appendix B.4 is titled as a proof of Corollary 3 but proves the almost-everywhere singleton claim behind Corollary 2, while Appendix D.2 separately proves Corollary 3. The reverse-mode calculation on page 22 also drops a transpose in one middle expression.

method.core_idea: Lift nonsmooth derivatives of a contractive fixed-point iteration to compact sets of matrices, study the resulting affine iterated-function system in Hausdorff geometry, and show that its fixed attractor is a conservative Jacobian of the primal fixed-point map.
method.mechanism: Each conservative Jacobian pair [A,B] acts on a candidate parameter Jacobian J by AJ+B. Uniform contraction of every A gives a contractive set map and a unique compact attractor. Stability to the vanishing perturbation J_F(x_k,theta)-J_F(xbar,theta) connects the moving piggyback recursion to that attractor. Conservative-calculus closure transfers derivative meaning through the fixed-point identity, almost-everywhere singleton properties recover classical derivatives, and a selection-regularity lemma yields a linear rate.
assumptions: F is locally Lipschitz and path differentiable jointly in state and parameter, with a nonempty locally bounded closed-graph conservative Jacobian.
Every x-block A in the selected J_F has operator norm at most one common rho<1 globally, or eventually in a neighborhood reached by the primal iterates.
The initialization is Lipschitz and needs its own conservative Jacobian; this clause is explicit in the final conference paper but omitted from the pinned arXiv v1 Assumption 1.
Set-valued derivative packets are compact, and convergence is measured by Hausdorff distance or the one-sided gap.
Classical derivative convergence is only for parameters in a full-measure set where every countably many iterate maps and the solution map are differentiable.
The linear-rate result additionally assumes a continuous semialgebraic finite selection representation whose component Jacobians are L-Lipschitz.
Forward-backward applications require a valid path-differentiable proximal map and strong convexity of f or g; Douglas-Rachford requires the cited strong-convexity and smoothness conditions.
The heavy-ball counterexample deliberately violates contractivity of the generalized state-Jacobian packet despite primal linear convergence.

techniques.role: Provides nonsmooth chain rules compatible with automatic differentiation and agrees with classical Jacobians almost everywhere.
Represents propagated parameter Jacobians as an iterated function system of affine matrix maps.
Uses the uniform x-block norm bound to obtain a unique compact fixed derivative set.
Controls moving Jacobian packets through one-sided distance to the packet at the primal fixed point.
Turns semialgebraic active-selection stability into a local Lipschitz bound for conservative Jacobians.
Converts full Jacobian convergence into forward JVP and reverse VJP convergence.
Instantiates the framework for forward-backward, Douglas-Rachford, and intended ADMM recursions.
Uses a product of individually admissible heavy-ball Jacobians to expose joint spectral instability.

evaluations.metric: One-sided gap from propagated conservative Jacobians to a compact fixed set and almost-everywhere convergence of classical Jacobians.
evaluations.result: The gap tends to zero for every parameter, while classical Jacobians, JVPs, and convergent-terminal-cotangent VJPs converge for almost every parameter.
evaluations.baseline: Smooth piggyback derivative convergence and nonsmooth implicit differentiation.

evaluations.result: For each theta and epsilon>0, the paper gives an existential C(sqrt(rho)+epsilon)^k bound.
evaluations.baseline: Qualitative gap convergence under closed-graph conservative Jacobians.

evaluations.setting: Forward-backward Lasso and purported Ridge, Douglas-Rachford sparse inverse covariance, and ADMM trend filtering, each with 100 random replicates and 2,000 iterations.
evaluations.metric: Median norm distance of iterates and propagated Jacobians to the final iterate, with first and last decile bands over the first 1,000 steps.
evaluations.result: All eight plotted curves decrease approximately linearly on log scale, but the Ridge notebook implements an unsquared l2 penalty and a stale step size, and the final iterate is used as an unverified proxy for the exact solution and derivative.
evaluations.baseline: No direct implicit-differentiation, finite-difference, runtime, or memory baseline.

evaluations.setting: Piecewise-quadratic heavy-ball and fixed-step gradient descent initialized at the kink.
evaluations.metric: Magnitude of the parameter derivative over 200 iterations.
evaluations.result: Gradient-descent derivatives decay while a selected heavy-ball derivative sequence grows geometrically; the four-step matrix product has spectral radius 9/8.
evaluations.baseline: Stable fixed-step gradient descent on the same piecewise quadratic.

limitations: Author-stated: the framework is built around strict contraction and leaves broader noncontractive algorithms for future work.
Author-stated: the conclusions are asymptotic and the local-contraction relaxation begins only after the primal trajectory enters a suitable neighborhood.
Reviewer inference: almost-everywhere convergence does not determine what a concrete AD implementation returns at a chosen nondifferentiable parameter.
Reviewer inference: the linear-rate constant is existential and does not provide a practical stopping rule or uniform finite-depth error certificate.
Reviewer inference: the pinned arXiv source omits the initialization-Jacobian clause later added to the final conference Assumption 1.
Reviewer inference: the Douglas-Rachford and ADMM appendix formulas contain sign, identity-block, transpose, conjugacy, and dimensional errors.
Reviewer inference: the trend-filtering symbols swap the smooth and nonsmooth functions and arXiv v1 falsely calls the l1 norm strongly convex.
Reviewer inference: the heavy-ball appendix falsely claims every parameterized iterate remains equal to its initialization, although only the theta=0 trajectory is needed.
Reviewer inference: the official notebook's Ridge code implements a different penalty and depends on stale state from a prior cell.
Reviewer inference: experiments use the last numerical iterate as ground truth and provide no finite-difference derivative check, runtime comparison, or exact uncertainty interval.
failure_modes: The primal map converges but its available generalized Jacobian packet is not jointly contractive.
An inertial method switches among locally stable derivative branches whose matrix products have joint spectral radius above one.
A parameter lies on an active-set boundary, so different equivalent implementations select different propagated derivatives.
The desired map is averaged or nonexpansive with rho=1 rather than strictly contractive.
The active selection family is not finite semialgebraic or its smooth pieces lack Lipschitz Jacobians, removing the stated linear rate.
A local trajectory never reaches or later leaves the neighborhood where the derivative packet is contractive.
Incorrect reflected-prox parameter blocks are implemented from Equations 24-25.
The ADMM dual derivation is copied literally despite its missing conjugate, transpose, variable, and squared-norm terms.
The notebook Ridge section is run independently before Xnorm exists, or after another experiment supplies a different stale Xnorm.
The plotted final iterate is not accurate enough to serve as the fixed-point or derivative reference.
reusable_insights: Analyze nonsmooth unrolling as a compact-set dynamical system when a single derivative is not well defined.
Track one-sided gap separately from Hausdorff convergence; attraction into a valid derivative set need not identify every point of that set.
Check the joint spectral behavior of derivative matrices, not only convergence of the primal iteration or stability of each branch in isolation.
Separate generic almost-everywhere guarantees from behavior at the exact kinks used by an application or test case.
Treat the initialization map as part of the differentiated program and state its conservative Jacobian explicitly.
Use a selection-activity argument to obtain local derivative regularity when nonsmooth pieces are finite and definable.
Validate proximal formulas by state and parameter block dimensions before composing conservative Jacobians.
Make notebooks cell-order independent by recomputing every problem-specific scale after regenerating data.
Verify that an experimental proximal operator matches the penalty printed in the paper, especially squared versus unsquared norms.
Use analytic solutions or strict residual tolerances rather than the last iterate as derivative ground truth.
open_questions: Can derivative convergence be proved for averaged nonexpansive maps or monotone-operator splittings without strict contraction?
What conditions on a generalized Jacobian packet characterize stability through its joint spectral radius rather than a common operator-norm bound?
Can one predict the particular conservative derivative chosen by PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow at exceptional parameters?
Is there a nonasymptotic, computable stopping certificate for piggyback Jacobians under local selection regularity?
How should the theory extend to stochastic iterations, random reshuffling, and variance-reduced solvers?
Can momentum schemes be differentiated safely by modifying damping or selecting a stable generalized derivative oracle?
Does the piggyback attractor contain useful derivatives not represented by the implicit set, or are the extra cross-compositions mainly pathological?
Can the affine-set proof and the Douglas-Rachford/ADMM appendices be formally restated with all self-map, dimensional, conjugacy, and transpose conditions explicit?
Do corrected Ridge and trend-filtering experiments preserve the displayed derivative convergence rates under independently computed references?
How do one-step and implicit estimators trade bias, memory, and stability against full nonsmooth unrolling at finite solver depth?

competitive_landscape.title: Conservative set valued fields, automatic differentiation, stochastic gradient method and deep learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Bolte and Pauwels introduce conservative fields and the nonsmooth AD calculus used here. The reviewed paper adds a fixed-point attractor and derivative-convergence theory for contractive iterative solvers rather than establishing the general calculus itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit differentiation of Lasso-type models for hyperparameter optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Bertrand et al. give a scalable support-aware implicit estimator and empirical hyperparameter optimization for Lasso-type problems. The reviewed paper is more general and explains unrolled derivative convergence, but it is less operational and provides no matched hypergradient performance comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient and Modular Implicit Differentiation
competitive_landscape.difference: Blondel et al. automate implicit differentiation from user-specified optimality conditions and decouple the derivative from the forward solver. It avoids long unrolling but relies on an implicit linear solve and predominantly smooth differentiable conditions; the reviewed work instead studies what nonsmooth unrolling converges to.

competitive_landscape.title: Nonsmooth Implicit Differentiation for Machine Learning and Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Bolte et al. prove a nonsmooth implicit-function theorem with conservative Jacobians under generalized invertibility. The reviewed paper connects repeated algorithmic differentiation to a possibly larger affine fixed set and requires iterative contraction instead of only pointwise implicit invertibility.

competitive_landscape.title: On the complexity of nonsmooth automatic differentiation
competitive_landscape.difference: Bolte et al. analyze forward and reverse computational overhead for nonsmooth definable programs and show a dimension-independent reverse-mode overhead. It complements rather than replaces the reviewed paper's asymptotic correctness analysis for iterative fixed points.

competitive_landscape.title: The Curse of Unrolling: Rate of Differentiating Through Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Scieur et al. derive nonasymptotic Jacobian rates and expose a burn-in versus asymptotic-speed tradeoff for smooth quadratic gradient and Chebyshev iterations. Its scope is narrower and smooth, but its finite-depth calibration addresses a practical question left existential by the reviewed paper.

competitive_landscape.title: One-step differentiation of iterative algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: Bolte, Pauwels, and Vaiter replace full unrolling with a one-step or Jacobian-free estimator and analyze its approximation for fast solvers and bilevel optimization. It directly targets the memory and computational burden that the reviewed full piggyback recursion does not benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: Derivatives of Stochastic Gradient Descent in parametric optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Iutzeler, Pauwels, and Vaiter extend derivative-iterate analysis to strongly convex SGD, proving mean-square noise-ball behavior for constant steps and O(log(k)^2/k) rates for decaying steps. This covers random recursion and explicit rates outside the deterministic contractive setting reviewed here.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first joint answer for nonsmooth fixed-point unrolling: a set-valued limiting object for piggyback derivatives, proof that it is a conservative Jacobian of the fixed-point map, almost-everywhere convergence of classical forward and reverse derivatives, a linear rate for semialgebraic selections, proximal-splitting applications, and a heavy-ball failure mode.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The affine compact-set construction genuinely links iterative nonsmooth AD to conservative differentiation and distinguishes its attractor from the smaller pointwise implicit set. The almost-everywhere reduction and heavy-ball switching example make the correctness boundary unusually explicit. Later work on finite unrolling rates, one-step estimators, nonsmooth AD complexity, and stochastic derivative recursions treats this paper as a foundation while addressing regimes it leaves open.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The set-valued attractor viewpoint is a real and reusable advance over the preceding nonsmooth implicit theorem, especially because it explains both generic classical convergence and exceptional implementation dependence. Its practical reach should not be overstated: strict packet contraction is strong, finite-depth constants are not calibrated, and several source formulas and the official Ridge artifact are wrong. The core theorem appears repairable and conceptually durable, while the proximal appendix and empirical panels require corrected derivations and reruns before being used as validation.
